questions.question: How does React decide when a component re-renders?
questions.answer: A component re-renders when its state changes, when its parent re-renders, or when a context it reads changes. Props changing is a consequence of the parent re-rendering, not a trigger on its own. React.memo skips a re-render when props are shallowly equal.

questions.question: What does the dependency array of useEffect do, and what goes wrong when it's incomplete?
questions.answer: It tells React when to re-run the effect: after a render in which any listed value changed. Leaving a value out means the effect keeps using a stale copy of it from an earlier render (a stale closure), which causes bugs like outdated data or intervals that never see new state.

questions.question: Why do list items need stable keys?
questions.answer: Keys tell React which item is which between renders. With stable keys it moves existing elements and their state; with index keys, inserting or reordering makes React reuse the wrong element, so input values and local state end up on the wrong row.

questions.question: When would you use useLayoutEffect instead of useEffect?
questions.answer: When you must measure or change the DOM before the browser paints, for example positioning a tooltip from an element's size. It runs synchronously after DOM updates and blocks painting, so use it only when a visible flicker would otherwise happen.

questions.question: When does lifting state up stop scaling, and what do you reach for instead?
questions.answer: When many distant components need the same state and passing props through layers becomes noisy. Context works for low-frequency values like theme or the current user; for frequently changing shared state, a small store or a server-state library avoids re-rendering large trees.

questions.question: Explain the event loop, including microtasks.
questions.answer: JavaScript runs one task at a time on the call stack. When the stack is empty, all queued microtasks run (promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) before the next macrotask (timers, I/O, events). That's why a resolved promise's then() runs before a setTimeout(…, 0) queued earlier.

questions.question: What is a closure? Give a practical use.
questions.answer: A closure is a function together with the variables it captured from the scope where it was created. They keep private state, for example a counter factory or a debounce function that remembers its timer between calls.

questions.question: Debounce versus throttle: what's the difference and when do you use each?
questions.answer: Debounce waits until calls stop for a set time, then runs once (search-as-you-type). Throttle runs at most once per interval while calls keep coming (scroll or resize handlers). Both limit how often expensive work happens.

questions.question: How does 'this' get its value?
questions.answer: By how the function is called: a method call sets it to the object, a plain call leaves it undefined in strict mode, new sets it to the new object, and call/apply/bind set it explicitly. Arrow functions don't have their own 'this'; they use the surrounding one.

questions.question: What are generics with constraints? Show a real use.
questions.answer: Generics let a function work over many types while keeping them linked; a constraint limits which types are allowed. For example function pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] only accepts real keys of the object and returns that property's exact type.

questions.question: What's the difference between unknown and any?
questions.answer: Both accept any value, but unknown forces you to narrow it (with typeof, instanceof or a schema) before using it, while any switches type checking off. Use unknown for untrusted input such as JSON or caught errors.

questions.question: What is a discriminated union and why is it useful?
questions.answer: A union of object types that share a literal field, such as { status: 'ok', data } | { status: 'error', message }. Checking that field narrows the type, so the compiler knows which properties exist, and a switch can be checked for exhaustiveness.

questions.question: Server Components and Client Components: where does each run and when do you need 'use client'?
questions.answer: Server Components render on the server and send no JavaScript for themselves; they can read data directly. Client Components also render on the server for the first HTML, then hydrate in the browser. You need 'use client' for state, effects, event handlers or browser APIs.

questions.question: How do you show fresh data after a mutation in the App Router?
questions.answer: Do the mutation in a Server Action, then invalidate what changed (revalidatePath or a tag-based revalidation) or refresh the router, so the next render reads current data. Optimistic UI can show the change immediately while the action runs.

questions.question: What does a Suspense boundary do for a slow part of a page?
questions.answer: It lets the rest of the page render and stream first, showing a fallback in the slow part's place. When the slow component's data is ready, its HTML streams in and replaces the fallback, so one slow query doesn't block the whole page.

questions.question: How does CSS specificity work?
questions.answer: When rules conflict, the more specific selector wins: inline styles, then IDs, then classes, attributes and pseudo-classes, then elements. With equal specificity the later rule wins. Cascade layers and !important change this order.

questions.question: Flexbox or Grid: how do you choose?
questions.answer: Flexbox lays things out in one direction and sizes items from their content (toolbars, rows of buttons). Grid controls rows and columns together (page layouts, card grids that must line up). They combine well: a grid of cards whose insides use flex.

questions.question: What causes layout shift and how do you prevent it?
questions.answer: Content that changes size after first paint: images or ads without dimensions, late web fonts, or content injected above what's already shown. Reserve space with width and height or aspect-ratio, use font-display with matched fallbacks, and insert new content below the fold or on user action.

questions.question: How would you cut a React app's initial bundle?
questions.answer: Measure first with a bundle analyser. Then split by route, lazy-load heavy components that aren't needed right away, replace large libraries with smaller ones or native APIs, and move work to the server so less JavaScript ships.

questions.question: How do you make a custom dropdown accessible?
questions.answer: Prefer a native select or a tested library. Otherwise: a button that toggles the list with aria-expanded, keyboard support (arrows, Enter, Escape), focus moved into the list and back, a listbox with options, and the selected value announced.

questions.question: What do you unit test and what do you cover with end-to-end tests?
questions.answer: Unit-test pure logic and edge cases where it's cheap and fast. Use component tests for behaviour as a user sees it. Keep a small set of end-to-end tests for the critical journeys (sign up, checkout) because they're slow but catch integration breaks.

questions.question: Why is blocking the event loop bad in Node.js, and what do you do about it?
questions.answer: One request's CPU-heavy work stops every other request from being handled until it finishes. Move heavy work to worker threads or a job queue, stream large data instead of loading it whole, and keep handlers asynchronous.

questions.question: Design a typeahead search box that stays fast.
questions.answer: Debounce input, cancel stale requests (AbortController) so results never arrive out of order, cache recent queries, and show results with keyboard navigation and accessible roles. On the server, use a prefix index and return small payloads; consider prefetching popular queries.

questions.question: How would you structure state for a large dashboard with live data?
questions.answer: Separate server state (cached, refetched, possibly via websockets) from UI state (filters, selection). Normalise entities, subscribe components to the narrow slices they show, and batch updates so a burst of messages doesn't re-render everything.
